scope_note: Full-source first pass for all targets and contexts. Boundary records preserve their XML limits and are not silently reclassified as current-period knowledge. Same-author continuations and prior accepted relationships are described but not recounted as new edges.

record_reviews.summary: Darwin replies to Quatrefages's 19 November letter by celebrating agreement on mutability, reporting the first edition's rapid sale and naming Lyell, Hooker, Carpenter and Huxley as converts. He asks Quatrefages to help find a French translator/editor and expressly says no answer is needed unless useful.
record_reviews.date_assessment: XML 1859-12-05, after the 24 November endpoint; the 19 November incoming is referenced but absent.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin is author; named naturalists and Madame Belloc are reported third-party voices.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: No prompt body survives and later post-publication reception cannot be backdated.

evidence.quote: The whole of the 1st. Edit (1250 copies) was sold on first day

record_reviews.summary: Darwin acknowledges Rolfe's £10 10s draft for Down charities and declines an invitation from Rolfe and Lady Cranworth because outings exhaust him for days. It is a short financial/social note with no scientific request.
record_reviews.date_assessment: XML 1858-11-10; no date or body for the referenced draft/invitation beyond Darwin's receipt.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin authored both retained paragraphs; Rolfe and Lady Cranworth are mentioned only as correspondents/inviters.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The incoming draft and invitation are not preserved as bodies; no reply edge is identified.

evidence.quote: I beg leave to acknowledge & thank you for the draft for 10100 for the Down charities.

record_reviews.summary: The firm answers Darwin's 15 June favour with Great North of Scotland Railway share capital, preference stock and dividend figures, then explains the North Eastern–Berwick charge shared across three lines. The final postscript says a favourable parcel of Berwick stock is currently available. Pencil/ink annotations alter some figures and options, so the printed body and authorial additions must remain separate.
record_reviews.date_assessment: XML 1859-06-17; explicitly says it replies to Darwin's 15 June enquiry. Receipt by Darwin is not separately dated.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Robert and John Shedden Scrimgeour & Co. authored the body; later Darwin annotations are excluded source layers and not firm prose.

evidence.quote: In reply to your favor of 15th. inst we beg to call your attention to the following information

record_reviews.summary: Darwin thanks Shaw for a Vienna Geographical Society diploma found at the Athenaeum and apologises for missing it earlier. The two-block note contains no scientific request or answer.
record_reviews.date_assessment: XML 1858-04-16; Shaw's note was found the previous day, but no full incoming source is preserved.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin authored the note; the Vienna Society and Shaw are named institutional context.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: No incoming prompt body or reply scope is identifiable.

evidence.quote: I was in London yesterday & only then found at the Athenæum Club, your note with the Diploma

record_reviews.summary: Darwin thanks Spencer for his Essays, praises the developmental-theory argument and explains that his own species work treats change as a naturalist rather than a general philosopher. He also discusses Spencer's Music and Expression articles and anticipates using his criticisms of style.
record_reviews.date_assessment: XML 1858-11-25; Spencer's present was received before composition but no delivery date is stated.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin is author; Spencer's arguments are reported and evaluated, not a surviving Spencer body.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: No Spencer incoming text is preserved; the letter acknowledges books/articles rather than answering a distinctive prompt.

evidence.quote: Your remarks on the general argument of the so-called Development Theory seem to me admirable.

record_reviews.summary: Swale answers Darwin after a 68-day postal journey with observations from Canterbury, New Zealand: bees were introduced only in 1852, yet peas, beans and clovers seeded before hive bees. He attributes fertilisation to native wasps, grasshoppers and wind, describes opening Lupine keels with a pin, and adds beekeeping and furze observations. Square-bracket restorations and missing words show manuscript extent; a CD note extracts the clover passage separately.
record_reviews.date_assessment: XML 1858-07-13; Swale states the communication took 68 days, establishing arrival of Darwin's prior request before composition but not Darwin's later reading date.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Swale authored the body. His claims about wasps, grasshoppers and local beekeeping are his reported observations; CD's annotations and extracted note are separate Darwin layers.

evidence.quote: Your interesting communication reached me quite safe after a postal journey of 68 days.

record_reviews.summary: Darwin asks Sykes to support Blyth's possible appointment as naturalist to the China Expedition, arguing that Blyth's broad natural-history experience makes him preferable to a mere collector. He says the note requires no acknowledgement or answer.
record_reviews.date_assessment: XML 1859-12-20, after the 24 November endpoint. The note itself excludes an expected answer and gives no receipt stage for Sykes.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin authored the three paragraphs; Blyth and Sykes are discussed in third person.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: Explicitly no-answer correspondence; no incoming prompt or current-period knowledge edge.

evidence.quote: As this note requires no acknowledgment or answer, I trust to your kindness to excuse my troubling you.

record_reviews.summary: Darwin thanks Thwaites for a 28 December letter about plant resistance and acclimatisation, quotes his distinction between alpine and lowland forms, asks about naturalised plants in Ceylon, and proposes cultivation experiments across elevations. It is a detailed request but the incoming Thwaites body is not present.
record_reviews.date_assessment: XML 1858-02-07; Thwaites's 28 December letter is referenced without an explicit year in the body.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin authored the source; Thwaites's plant observations are paraphrased and Darwin's uncertainty about hairiness is explicit.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: No preserved Thwaites prompt is available; later Thwaites correspondence must not be inferred from topic.

evidence.quote: I will quote this part of your note; for it was exactly a point on which I wanted information.

record_reviews.summary: The source is a brief Darwin note to Thwaites thanking him for information and continuing requests about Ceylon specimens and variation; its original date/extent are retained in the packet metadata. The body does not supply a new 1858-59 prompt or response.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Use the source's XML constraints and header rather than packet order; this record is outside the current endpoint and retained as context.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin is the author; any Thwaites material is reported rather than surviving incoming prose.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: No current-period relationship can be established from this boundary context.

record_reviews.summary: Darwin thanks Fanny for arranging Anne's return and burial, says her tenderness gave him consolation, asks where the grave lies and adds a postscript about her health. The grave-location sketch is mentioned in apparatus, not present inline.
record_reviews.date_assessment: XML 1851-04-25; composition follows the funeral arrangement, while receipt by Fanny is not shown.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin authored the body; the postscript is also Darwin text despite its placement. The grave sketch is separate evidence.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: No new prompt; this family exchange is already covered by earlier primary reading.

evidence.quote: I owe it to you that I am here.

record_reviews.summary: Fanny reports that she and Hensleigh completed Anne's burial at nine, describes Brodie and Miss Thorley's grief, and reassures Emma that Charles had arrived. She promises a Monday line and records Dr Gully's enquiry in P4. This is Fanny's eyewitness account, not Emma's or Darwin's voice.
record_reviews.date_assessment: XML 1851-04-25; the burial and return travel are same-day events, with no separate Darwin receipt date.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Fanny authored the body; Hensleigh, Brodie, Miss Thorley and Dr Gully are reported participants.

evidence.quote: We went at 9 o’clock & I think every thing was rightly arranged as you would have wished

record_reviews.summary: Fanny thanks Emma and Charles for letters found at home, recalls helping Charles leave Malvern and the comfort of their arrival, and describes the children's grief and her own continued availability. She reports Effie, Hannah and other family reactions and closes with a note to the Tollets.
record_reviews.date_assessment: XML 1851-04-28; the letters were found on Saturday after the journey, but exact delivery times remain unstated.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Fanny is author; family members' statements are reported voices. The apparatus identifies named relations but does not turn them into separate letters.

evidence.quote: I cannot tell you the comfort & even pleasure, sad as it was, that they gave me

record_reviews.summary: Darwin thanks Fanny for news of Erasmus's fever, asks for a brief update and recalls the comfort she gave during Anne's illness. It is a three-block health acknowledgement.
record_reviews.date_assessment: XML 1854-08-18; date inferred editorially from Erasmus's illness and related Hooker letter.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin authored the body; Fanny, Caroline and Josiah are referenced but no incoming text survives.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: No new prompt or current-period relationship.

evidence.quote: We are infinitely obliged to you, after all your fatigue, writing to us about poor dear old Erasmus’ illness.

record_reviews.summary: Darwin asks Quatrefages for details of Flourens's claimed third-generation sterile dog/wolf/jackal hybrids and help obtaining Dureau de la Malle's horse-breed pamphlet. He offers a Journal of Researches copy and notes uncertainty about Quatrefages's English. The earlier Quatrefages note and later reply are missing.
record_reviews.date_assessment: XML 1855-11-20; editorial notes establish the date from Darwin's reading of Souvenirs and distinguish later sending of Journal.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin is author; Flourens and Dureau de la Malle are cited publications, not incoming voices.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: No preserved Quatrefages answer; 2571 is later and outside the endpoint.

evidence.quote: whether the sterility of these hybrids in the 3d generation was ascertained in several cases

record_reviews.summary: Darwin asks Thwaites for Ceylon pigeon and poultry breeds, skins and native names, including a bird-skinner who could collect old birds. He explains the relevance to variation and domestic breeds, while apologising for the scale of the request.
record_reviews.date_assessment: XML 1855-12-10; requests are prospective and do not establish later receipt of specimens.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin authored all six blocks; Ceylon informants and fanciers are hypothetical/prospective.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: No incoming Thwaites answer or specimens are preserved here; later Variation citations are not a dated prompt.

evidence.quote: whether there are any Fanciers in Ceylon

record_reviews.source_kind: Darwin-authored outgoing institutional letter / earlier context
record_reviews.summary: Darwin thanks Shaw for useful introductions and asks him to approach Consul Brand about collecting poultry skins in Angola. He extends the search to Arabia/Aden, mentions Erhardt and Sykes, and says he has written to every major region except Arabia.
record_reviews.date_assessment: XML 1855-12-25; recipient is conjectured from provenance and date is relational, so the source remains an evidentiary hold.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin authored the body; Brand, Erhardt and Sykes are proposed intermediaries, not incoming authors.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: No response or collected specimen source is preserved; no current-period edge.

evidence.quote: I have now written to each chief quarter of the world, except Arabia.

record_reviews.summary: Darwin thanks Quatrefages for the anticipated Flourens information, says he sent Journal through Williams & Norgate, and explains that his variation work will take years because he is maintaining many domestic varieties. It follows 1782F but does not preserve a Quatrefages answer.
record_reviews.date_assessment: XML 1856-01-04; date established relationally to the November 1855 request.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin authored both blocks; Flourens's prospective information is reported.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: No incoming body or new period link; later 2571 cannot be backdated.

evidence.quote: The information, which you hope to obtain from M. Flourens will be of the greatest value to me

record_reviews.summary: Darwin thanks Thwaites for receiving his Oxford-linked request warmly, asks for Ceylon alpine/elevation variation and naturalised plants, and requests skins or skeletons of non-English pigeons, ducks and poultry. He explicitly frames the species work as weighing common descent against difficulties.
record_reviews.date_assessment: XML 1856-03-08; no receipt date for a Thwaites answer is supplied.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin authored the five blocks; Hooker and Kellaart are cited as possible helpers.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: No incoming Thwaites prompt is preserved; this is an initiated request and earlier context.

evidence.quote: The courrse of my work makes me more & more sceptical on the eternal immutability of species

record_reviews.summary: Darwin formally thanks Spencer for his copy of Principles of Psychology. The single retained block records that the book had already been on Darwin's reading list; it contains no scientific question.
record_reviews.date_assessment: XML 1856-03-11; exact date is supplied, outside current period.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin authored the formal third-person note; Spencer's book is the received object, not an incoming letter body.

evidence.quote: only about a fortnight since he wrote down in his list of books to be read
